\chapter{Review --- Three Verbs That Behave}
\label{ch:spanish-review-ordinary-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{162}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can use all three verbs and say what they have in common: the sentence is about the one doing it.}

Three origins - tidy, reshaped, and genuinely unknown - and the shared shape about to be broken.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[Practice]{Review — three verbs that behave}

\label{lesson:ES-C35-repaso-tres}



\begin{quote}
Nothing new here. Name the three verbs of the last three chapters: to take, to ask, to help.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
All three work the way you expect, and it is worth naming that out loud \textbf{before} the next chapter, where one does not.

In each of them, \textbf{you} are the one doing it. You take. You ask. You help. The person doing the verb is the person the sentence is about — exactly as in English, and exactly as in every verb you have met since \emph{hablo}.

Hold on to that. It is about to be worth money.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
Three origins, three very different kinds of story:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ayudar} is the tidy one. Latin \emph{adiūtāre} $\to$ English \textbf{aid}. Same word, two roads, and you can still hear it.
  \item \textbf{preguntar} is the reshaped one — \emph{percontārī}, to sound a depth with a pole. Asking as measuring how deep something goes.
  \item \textbf{tomar} is the honest gap. It has \textbf{no agreed origin at all.} The verb Latin actually handed down for \textquotedblleft{}take\textquotedblright{} was \emph{coger}, and \emph{coger} turned coarse across much of Latin America — so an everyday word had to come from somewhere, and nobody is sure where.
\end{itemize}

Not every word has a clean story. A course that pretended otherwise would be inventing them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} the three verbs, then one sentence with each
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which one has no settled origin? (\emph{Tomar}.) In all three, who is the sentence about? (\textbf{The one doing it}.) Next chapter: a verb where that stops being true.
\end{tcolorbox}
